## Web Searcher: evidence base for loading, progress and perceived performance

Research question: "Research the state of the art in web visual design vocabulary, to extend the reference library of an agent-run pipeline that forges bespoke personal portfolio sites (PIIIX-org/portfolio.me). The pipeline already documents 32 named visual styles across 7 families (surface/material, structural, atmospheric, motion-native, technical/data, textural, reductive) and 72 rendering techniques across 6 groups (GPU/rendering, post-processing, CSS+SVG native, motion/input, whole-page, typographic craft). Its documented GAP is everything about PRESENTING INFORMATION — it has no data-visualization vocabulary and no component-pattern vocabulary at all.

COVER ALL SIX AREAS:

1. DATA AND INFORMATION VISUALIZATION — chart type selection and when each is the right encoding; perceptual ranking of visual encodings (position/length/angle/area/color) and the research behind it; sequential, diverging and categorical color scale construction (including OKLCH/perceptually-uniform approaches and colorblind-safe palettes); small multiples; sparklines and in-line micro-charts; dashboard and stat-tile layout patterns; data storytelling and scrollytelling (scroll-linked chart transitions, annotation layers); editorial data-graphics conventions from newsrooms (NYT, FT, Pudding, Reuters); table design at density (tabular numerals, decimal alignment, hairline rules, sticky headers); how to present evidence and provenance so figures are checkable; accessible charts (screen-reader alternatives, non-color encoding, focus order).

2. COMPONENT AND CONTAINER PATTERNS — cards and their many failure modes; documented ALTERNATIVES to the card grid for presenting a body of projects or work (editorial indexes, tables-as-index, list-with-hover-preview, timelines, maps, filmstrips, stacked/scroll-driven layouts, masonry critiques, single-item-at-a-time patterns, hub-and-spoke); drawers, sheets, side panels, bottom sheets and their platform conventions; modals versus inline expansion versus routed pages, and when each is correct; progressive disclosure patterns; accordions and details/summary; lists — dense, editorial, and interactive; empty, loading and error states as designed deliverables; navigation patterns beyond a top bar.

3. NEW AND EMERGING VISUAL STYLE MOVEMENTS — named aesthetic movements in web and interface design current as of 2025-2026 that are NOT in the list above; include their defining mechanics, their characteristic failure mode, and the condition under which they are the right choice. Also cover which looks now read as generic, templated, or AI-default (so they can be avoided), and the discourse on distinctive versus homogenized web design.

4. MOTION AND INTERACTION FOR THE ABOVE — how cards, drawers, lists and charts should actually behave; shared-element and container transforms; the View Transitions API; disclosure and expansion motion; chart entrance, transition and morphing animation; staggering and orchestration; scroll-linked and scroll-driven reveals; spring/physics versus duration-and-easing, and when each is right.

5. MICRO-INTERACTIONS AND MICRO-ANIMATION — the anatomy and principles of a micro-interaction; feedback, state change and affordance signalling; hover, focus, press and drag states; optimistic UI; haptics; sound; the timing, easing and duration ranges that read as responsive versus sluggish, with the research or platform guidance behind the numbers.

6. LOADING, PROGRESS AND PERCEIVED PERFORMANCE — skeleton screens versus spinners versus progress indicators and the evidence for each; designed preloaders; streaming and progressive rendering; optimistic and predictive loading; perceived-performance research including documented duration thresholds; layout-shift avoidance.

CONSTRAINTS THAT MAKE A FINDING USABLE — prefer and clearly flag findings that satisfy these, and flag ones that violate them:
- Web-native and implementable in HTML/CSS/SVG/canvas/WebGL. Note when a pattern is CSS/SVG-native (cheap) versus requiring a heavy runtime.
- Two-tier budget: a shell under 100KB (HTML, critical CSS, subset fonts, minimal JS) that paints alone with LCP under 1.5s, and a deferred heavy layer. Note byte cost and whether a technique can be deferred.
- Every technique must ship three states: full, a DESIGNED reduced-motion still (never `animation: none`), and a no-WebGL/no-canvas fallback.
- Accessibility is non-negotiable: WCAG contrast, keyboard operability, focus management (especially for drawers, sheets and modals — focus trap, restore, escape, inert background), screen-reader semantics, and non-color encodings.
- Self-hosted and vendored: no CDN in production, no third-party badge or chart services, no hotlinked stock imagery. Visuals are generated (CSS, SVG, canvas, WebGL, procedural) or generated-then-treated in-browser.
- Anti-template: the pipeline's core rule is that two runs must never look alike, so favour findings that support distinctiveness and explicitly name what has become a cliché.

DELIVERABLE — a survey report first: the landscape per area, with concrete named patterns, the mechanics of each, its documented failure mode, the condition under which it is right, and citations. Prefer primary and authoritative sources: peer-reviewed HCI and visualization research, Nielsen Norman Group, MDN and W3C/WAI-ARIA Authoring Practices, platform human-interface guidelines (Apple HIG, Material Design), the published work of newsroom graphics desks, and named practitioners — over listicles and SEO content. Where a number is claimed (a duration threshold, a byte weight, a perceptual ranking), attribute it to its source and note if it is folklore rather than measured. THEN, in a clearly separated final section, map the findings to the repo: which belong as new STYLES.md entries (four-part shape: mechanics / Implies / Fails / Right when), which as new or extended CRAFT.md technique groups (table shape: Technique / What it is / Where it earns its place), and which are new material entirely — flagging any that conflict with the existing rules."

Your angle: **evidence base for loading, progress and perceived performance** — Area 6, explicitly hunting numbers and their provenance. The skeleton-screen advantage is widely repeated but thinly measured, so this angle must separate actual studies (Miller, Card, Nielsen's response-time limits, the few controlled skeleton experiments) from folklore, and tie back to the pipeline's sub-100KB shell and 1.5s LCP budget via Core Web Vitals primary documentation.
Search query: `research evidence skeleton screens vs spinners vs progress bars perceived duration, Nielsen 0.1 1 10 second response time limits Miller 1968 Card 1991, progressive streaming rendering, optimistic UI, Core Web Vitals LCP and CLS layout shift avoidance`

## Task
Use WebSearch with the query above (or a refined version). Return the top 4-6 most relevant results.
Rank by relevance to the ORIGINAL question, not just the search query. Skip obvious SEO spam/content farms.
Include a short snippet capturing why each result is relevant.

Structured output only.

{"hookSpecificOutput":{"hookEventName":"SubagentStart","additionalContext":"PONYTAIL MODE ACTIVE — level: full

# Ponytail

You are a lazy senior developer. Lazy means efficient, not careless. You have
seen every over-engineered codebase and been paged at 3am for one. The best
code is the code never written.

## Persistence

ACTIVE EVERY RESPONSE. No drift back to over-building. Still active if
unsure. Off only: "stop ponytail" / "normal mode". Default: **full**.
Switch: `/ponytail lite|full|ultra`.

## The ladder

Stop at the first rung that holds:

1. **Does this need to exist at all?** Speculative need = skip it, say so in one line. (YAGNI)
2. **Already in this codebase?** A helper, util, type, or pattern that already lives here → reuse it. Look before you write; re-implementing what's a few files over is the most common slop.
3. **Stdlib does it?** Use it.
4. **Native platform feature covers it?** `<input type="date">` over a picker lib, CSS over JS, DB constraint over app code.
5. **Already-installed dependency solves it?** Use it. Never add a new one for what a few lines can do.
6. **Can it be one line?** One line.
7. **Only then:** the minimum code that works.

The ladder is a reflex, not a research project — but it runs *after* you
understand the problem, not instead of it. Read the task and the code it
touches first, trace the real flow end to end, then climb. Two rungs work →
take the higher one and move on. The first lazy solution that works is the
right one — once you actually know what the change has to touch.

**Bug fix = root cause, not symptom.** A report names a symptom. Before you
edit, grep every caller of the function you're about to touch. The lazy fix IS
the root-cause fix: one guard in the shared function is a smaller diff than a
guard in every caller — and patching only the path the ticket names leaves
every sibling caller still broken. Fix it once, where all callers route through.

## Rules

- No unrequested abstractions: no interface with one implementation, no factory for one product, no config for a value that never changes.
- No boilerplate, no scaffolding "for later", later can scaffold for itself.
- Deletion over addition. Boring over clever, clever is what someone decodes at 3am.
- Fewest files possible. Shortest working diff wins — but only once you understand the problem. The smallest change in the wrong place isn't lazy, it's a second bug.
- Complex request? Ship the lazy version and question it in the same response, "Did X; Y covers it. Need full X? Say so." Never stall on an answer you can default.
- Two stdlib options, same size? Take the one that's correct on edge cases. Lazy means writing less code, not picking the flimsier algorithm.
- Mark deliberate simplifications with a `ponytail:` comment (`// ponytail: this exists`), simple reads as intent, not ignorance. Shortcut with a known ceiling (global lock, O(n²) scan, naive heuristic)? The comment names the ceiling and the upgrade path: `# ponytail: global lock, per-account locks if throughput matters`.

## Output

Code first. Then at most three short lines: what was skipped, when to add it.
No essays, no feature tours, no design notes. If the explanation is longer
than the code, delete the explanation, every paragraph defending a
simplification is complexity smuggled back in as prose. Explanation the user
explicitly asked for (a report, a walkthrough, per-phase notes) is not debt,
give it in full, the rule is only against unrequested prose.

Pattern: `[code] → skipped: [X], add when [Y].`

## Intensity

| Level | What change |
|-------|------------|
| **full** | The ladder enforced. Stdlib and native first. Shortest diff, shortest explanation. Default. |

Example: "Add a cache for these API responses."
- full: "`@lru_cache(maxsize=1000)` on the fetch function. Skipped custom cache class, add when lru_cache measurably falls short."

## When NOT to be lazy

Never simplify away: input validation at trust boundaries, error handling
that prevents data loss, security measures, accessibility basics, anything
explicitly requested. User insists on the full version → build it, no
re-arguing.

Never lazy about understanding the problem. The ladder shortens the
solution, never the reading. Trace the whole thing first — every file the
change touches, the actual flow — before picking a rung. Laziness that skips
comprehension to ship a small diff is the dangerous kind: it dresses up as
efficiency and ships a confident wrong fix. Read fully, then be lazy.

Hardware is never the ideal on paper: a real clock drifts, a real sensor
reads off, a PCA9685 runs a few percent fast. Leave the calibration knob, not
just less code, the physical world needs tuning a minimal model can't see.

Lazy code without its check is unfinished. Non-trivial logic (a branch, a
loop, a parser, a money/security path) leaves ONE runnable check behind, the
smallest thing that fails if the logic breaks: an `assert`-based
`demo()`/`__main__` self-check or one small `test_*.py`. No frameworks, no
fixtures, no per-function suites unless asked. Trivial one-liners need no
test, YAGNI applies to tests too.

## Boundaries

Ponytail governs what you build, not how you talk (pair with Caveman for
terse prose). "stop ponytail" / "normal mode": revert. Level persists until
changed or session end.

The shortest path to done is the right path.
"}}

- _gstack-command: Router for the gstack skill suite. (gstack)
- academic-paper-composer: Systematic writing framework for philosophy and interdisciplinary academic papers from optimized outline to submission-ready manuscript. Use when users want to: (1) write a paper from a detailed outline, (2) ensure quality control during writing, (3) maintain consistency across chapters, (4) prepare a submission-ready manuscript, or (5) systematically execute a planned paper. Triggered by phrases like 'write the paper from this outline,' 'compose the full manuscript,' 'execute the outline,' or when users have completed strategic planning (academic-paper-strategist skill) and are ready to write. Takes optimized outline as input; outputs complete manuscript with iterative quality checks.
- academic-paper-strategist: Systematic strategic planning framework for philosophy and interdisciplinary academic papers targeting preprint platforms (PhilArchive, arXiv, PhilSci-Archive). Use when users want to: (1) plan a paper on a specific topic, (2) identify research gaps and assess originality, (3) develop optimized paper outlines, (4) prepare for preprint submission, or (5) understand platform requirements and writing standards. Triggered by phrases like 'plan a paper on,' 'help me design a paper about,' 'identify research gaps in,' 'is this idea original,' or when users need structured research planning. The skill guides through three phases: Platform Analysis (identifying target venue and studying sample papers), Theoretical Framework (AI-driven literature search and gap identification), and Outline Optimization (structured design with reviewer-perspective self-assessment). Each phase includes quality evaluation standards and validation checkpoints. Output: optimized detailed outline ready for systematic writing (use with academic-paper-composer skill).

Based on the search results, here's what controlled experiment evidence shows about skeleton screens versus spinners for perceived duration:

## Key Controlled Experiment Findings

When testing skeletons versus spinners and a blank control in random order, the skeleton performed the best in terms of perceived duration when shown to people using mobile devices (with a sample size of 80 individuals).

## Experimental Methodology

To mitigate bias, the app automatically randomized the order in which the different loading paradigms appeared, and also randomized the actual duration presented for each loading paradigm, so the duration didn't seem progressively longer or shorter. Participants were asked to complete nine different tests with three different durations for each of the three loading paradigms.

## Additional Research Evidence

The page using skeleton screens scored higher on average on both perceived speed and ease of navigation, though interestingly, people using the page with spinners were faster at finding the article when entering the site for the first time.

## Design Insights

Skeleton screens using motion that is slow and steady are perceived as shorter in duration than skeleton screens that use fast or rapid motion, though the study notes that sample sizes were small.

The research indicates that while both loading methods take the same actual time, skeleton screens create a psychological perception of faster loading compared to spinners.

Based on the search results, I found clear information about the provenance of the Nielsen response time limits:

## Provenance of the Response Time Limits

The basic advice regarding response times has been about the same for thirty years [Miller 1968; Card et al. 1991]: 0.1 second is about the limit for having the user feel that the system is reacting instantaneously, meaning that no special feedback is necessary except to display the result.

The three response time thresholds are:

1. **0.1 seconds**: 0.1 second is about the limit for having the user feel that the system is reacting instantaneously, meaning that no special feedback is necessary except to display the result.

2. **1.0 second**: 1.0 second is about the limit for the user's flow of thought to stay uninterrupted, even though the user will notice the delay.

3. **10 seconds**: 10 seconds is about the limit for keeping the user's attention focused on the dialogue.

## Original Sources

Miller, R. B. (1968). Response time in man-computer conversational transactions. This is the foundational research that established these response time categories.

Card, S. K., Robertson, G. G., and Mackinlay, J. D. (1991). The information visualizer: An information workspace. Proc. ACM CHI'91 Conf. (New Orleans, LA, 28 April-2 May), 181-188. This work by Card et al. reinforced and validated Miller's earlier findings.

Jakob Nielsen popularized and articulated these principles in his 1993 article "Response Times: The 3 Important Limits," which remains widely cited in user experience design today.

Based on the web.dev documentation, I found the information you're looking for regarding the Core Web Vitals thresholds:

## Largest Contentful Paint (LCP) - 2.5 seconds

To provide a good user experience, sites should strive to have Largest Contentful Paint of 2.5 seconds or less. To ensure you're hitting this target for most of your users, a good threshold to measure is the 75th percentile of page loads, segmented across mobile and desktop devices.

Largest Contentful Paint (LCP) is an important, stable Core Web Vital metric for measuring perceived load speed because it marks the point in the page load timeline when the page's main content has likely loaded—a fast LCP helps reassure the user that the page is useful.

## Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS) - 0.1

To provide a good user experience, pages should maintain a CLS of 0.1. or less. It's an important, user-centric metric for measuring visual stability because it helps quantify how often users experience unexpected layout shifts.

The research behind the CLS threshold of 0.1 is documented in the methodology: In internal testing, they found that levels of shift from 0.15 and higher were consistently perceived as disruptive, while shifts of 0.1 and lower were noticeable but not excessively disruptive.

I've found comprehensive information from Nielsen Norman Group on progress indicators, percent-done animations, and loading feedback guidelines. Here's a summary of their key recommendations:

## Progress Indicators Overview

Wait animations, such as percent-done bars and spinners, inform users of the current working state and make the process more tolerable by reducing uncertainty. Users experience higher satisfaction with a site and are willing to wait longer when the site uses a dynamic progress indicator.

## When to Use Percent-Done Indicators

Percent-done progress indicators should be used for longer processes that take 10 or more seconds. Percent-done progress indicators are the most informative type of wait-animation feedback. They show the current progress, how much has already been accomplished, and how much is left. They convey important information about (approximately) how long the wait time is.

## Benefits of Progress Indicators

Progress indicators have three main advantages: they reassure the user that the system has not crashed but is working on his or her problem; they indicate approximately how long the user can be expected to wait, thus allowing the user to do other activities during long waits; and they provide something for the user to look at, thus making the wait less painful.

## Guidelines for Complex Applications

Communicate percentage of work done or time remaining for any wait that exceeds 10 seconds. Progress indicators that provide details such as time elapsed (or steps completed) and time or steps remaining make long waits more tolerable and increase user confidence.

These guidelines emphasize the importance of providing clear, informative feedback to users during loading and processing operations.

I found comprehensive information on progressive rendering, streaming HTML, and perceived performance optimization. Here are the key findings:

## Progressive Rendering and Streaming

HTML streaming means sending HTML to the browser chunk-by-chunk, as soon as it's ready, rather than waiting until the entire document is completed. The idea is simple: give the web browser a head start in downloading and rendering the page by flushing out early and multiple times.

## Out-of-Order Early Flush

The strategy of out-of-order flushing of asynchronous fragments can significantly improve the load time and perceived load time of a page. HTML chunks can be delivered in any order with out-of-order streaming and a tiny trailing JavaScript payload to swap the HTML into its final location.

## Performance Benefits

This feature allows the HTML and external resources to be downloaded earlier, and for parts of the page to be rendered earlier. As a result, both the actual load time and the perceived load time improve. The most significant benefit of streaming is improved perceived performance.

## Optimistic UI and Fallbacks

Streaming eliminates this restriction by allowing fallback UI elements to be rendered in place of data-dependent components until the latter can be delivered to the browser. You can render light-weight placeholders (loading skeletons) where data is pending, and then swap in real content seamlessly.

## Modern Implementation

Progressive Server-Side Rendering (PSSR) bridges the gap between Server-Side Rendering and Client-Side Rendering by progressively streaming HTML content, improving perceived load times. React can hydrate interactive chunks as soon as they are received, reducing idle time.

## Key Evidence and Criticism on Skeleton Screens

### The Critical Viget Study

The Viget study tested skeleton screens with 136 people, and found the skeleton screen performed the worst by all metrics. Users in the skeleton screen group took longer to complete the task, were more likely to evaluate their wait time negatively, and guessed that the wait time had been longer than users who saw the loading spinner or a blank screen. This represents the main criticism that skeleton screens are "no better than" alternative loading indicators.

### Counter-Evidence: Bill Chung's Study

However, when testing skeletons versus spinners and a blank control, the skeleton performed the best in terms of perceived duration when shown to people using mobile devices (with a sample size of 80 individuals). Skeleton screens also performed best on the emotional level, with participants being the most happy with skeleton screen loads, and least happy overall with a blank screen.

### Other Supporting Evidence

An exploratory study by Mejtoft and test results on skeleton screens by Bill suggest that skeleton screens are perceived faster and are easier to navigate.

results.title: Response Time Limits: 0.1s / 1s / 10s — Jakob Nielsen (NN/g, 1993)
results.snippet: THE provenance source for the three numbers everyone quotes. Nielsen states plainly that "the basic advice regarding response times has been about the same for thirty years [Miller 1968; Card et al. 1991]" — i.e. 0.1s = feels instantaneous (no feedback needed beyond the result), 1.0s = flow of thought stays uninterrupted (delay noticed, no special feedback), 10s = limit of attention on the dialogue (beyond it, give a percent-done indicator and let the user do something else). Citable primaries: Miller, R.B. (1968) "Response time in man-computer conversational transactions"; Card, Robertson & Mackinlay (1991) "The information visualizer: an information workspace", CHI'91, 181–188. Critically for the report's folklore/measured split: these are perceptual-psychology thresholds from mainframe-era HCI, NOT web-loading measurements — cite them for interaction latency (hover, press, disclosure, chart transitions) and flag that extending them to page loads is extrapolation. Directly sets the ceiling for micro-interaction timings in Area 5 and the "when does a loading affordance need to exist at all" question in Area 6.

results.title: How the Core Web Vitals metrics thresholds were defined — web.dev (Chrome team)
results.snippet: Primary documentation of WHY the CWV numbers are what they are, which is exactly the provenance the angle demands. Explains the threshold methodology (quality-of-experience research, achievability across the HTTP Archive corpus, 75th-percentile measurement segmented mobile/desktop) and gives the CLS derivation directly: internal testing found shifts of 0.15 and above were "consistently perceived as disruptive" while 0.1 and below were "noticeable but not excessively disruptive." Anchors LCP ≤ 2.5s and CLS ≤ 0.1 as measured-and-justified rather than folklore. Note the tension to flag for the pipeline: the repo budget of LCP < 1.5s is STRICTER than the documented good threshold — that is a self-imposed target, not a standards number, and should be labelled as such. Companion primaries for the same numbers: web.dev/articles/lcp, web.dev/articles/cls, web.dev/articles/optimize-cls (layout-shift avoidance: dimension attributes on media, reserved space for injected content, font-swap strategy).

results.title: A Bone to Pick with Skeleton Screens — Viget (controlled study, n=136)
results.snippet: The strongest published counter-evidence to the "skeletons feel faster" consensus, and the single most useful citation for separating measured results from repetition. In a randomised test of skeleton vs. spinner vs. blank screen with 136 participants, the skeleton screen performed WORST on every metric measured: users took longer to complete the task, were more likely to rate the wait negatively, and estimated the wait as longer than the spinner or blank-screen groups. Because it contradicts the received wisdom (and Chung's and Mejtoft's results), it establishes that the skeleton advantage is condition-dependent, not a law — the correct framing for a STYLES/CRAFT entry is a documented failure mode ("skeleton whose geometry does not match the final layout, or which persists past ~1s, reads as a stall and inflates perceived duration"), not a blanket recommendation. Also flags the byte/complexity argument: a skeleton that mispredicts final layout causes the very CLS it was supposed to prevent.

results.title: The effect of skeleton screens: users' perception of speed and ease of navigation — Mejtoft et al., ECCE '18 (ACM)
results.snippet: The peer-reviewed counterweight to Viget, and the only proper conference-published skeleton experiment in this area (Proceedings of the 36th European Conference on Cognitive Ergonomics, ACM DL). Found the skeleton-screen page scored higher on average for both perceived speed and perceived ease of navigation — but with the honest wrinkle that spinner-group participants were actually FASTER at locating the target article on first visit. Pair with Viget and with Bill Chung's independently-run mobile test (n=80, randomised paradigm order AND randomised durations, skeleton best on perceived duration and on self-reported emotional response, blank screen worst) to show the state of the evidence is: three small studies, conflicting directions, no meta-analysis, effect sizes modest. That is the accurate provenance verdict for the report — "weakly and inconsistently supported", not "proven". Chung's secondary finding is the actionable craft detail: slow, steady skeleton motion is perceived as shorter than fast or rapid motion (small n — flag as suggestive).

results.title: Progress Indicators Make a Slow System Less Insufferable — NN/g
results.snippet: Authoritative source for the indicator-selection rule keyed to duration, and for the three classic benefits (reassures the system has not crashed; sets expectation of how long, freeing the user to do something else; gives something to look at, making the wait less painful — these trace back to Myers 1985 via Nielsen's Usability Engineering). The operative numbered guidance: use a percent-done indicator for processes of 10 seconds or more, because it is the most informative wait feedback — it conveys progress made, work remaining, and approximate duration; below that, a looping/indeterminate animation suffices; below ~1s, show nothing (a flashed spinner is worse than no spinner). NN/g also reports users express higher satisfaction and tolerate longer waits with a dynamic indicator. Companion NN/g pages worth citing alongside: "Visibility of System Status" (Heuristic #1), "Designing for Long Waits and Interruptions", and the NN/g video "Skeleton Screens vs. Progress Bars vs. Spinners".

results.title: Effective Skeleton Screens — Tim Kadlec
results.snippet: A named web-performance practitioner explicitly reconciling the contradictory skeleton evidence (Viget vs. Chung/Mejtoft) into implementable conditions, which is what turns the studies into a CRAFT.md row. Argues the wins and losses are explained by execution, not by the pattern: the skeleton must closely mirror the geometry of the content that replaces it (otherwise you get a jarring swap and real CLS), must not over-promise more content than arrives, and must be reserved for waits long enough to warrant it — otherwise it advertises slowness. Web-native and cheap in the pipeline's terms: a skeleton is pure CSS/HTML boxes, inlinable in the sub-100KB shell with effectively zero JS, degrades to a designed static still under prefers-reduced-motion (grey blocks with no shimmer, satisfying the "never animation: none" rule), and needs no canvas/WebGL fallback at all. Pairs naturally with streaming/progressive HTML rendering as the alternative that removes the need for a placeholder entirely — see eBay's "Async Fragments: Rediscovering Progressive HTML Rendering with Marko" (innovation.ebayinc.com) for the out-of-order early-flush technique and its measured effect on real and perceived load time.
